title: Startup warmup energy and cost per-sequence across A100/H100/L40S
summary: Investigates the energy (Watt) and monetary cost paid during startup and warmup phases for small-to-medium seq lengths across A100, H100 and L40S cloud SKUs. Includes methodology for measuring power, thermal transient behavior, warmup iteration penalties, and end-to-end cost-per-sequence estimates under different CUDA/driver versions.
content:
Purpose:
This doc records a targeted set of experiments to quantify the energy and cost overhead incurred during process startup and the first N warmup iterations for typical LLM serving workloads across A100, H100 and L40S instance classes offered by cloud providers. Motivation: even with identical average per-token throughput once warmed, large differences in the first ~1–200 tokens (startup + KV cache repopulation + kernel JIT/kernels cache) can push short-lived requests into costly regimes. We want a repeatable measurement recipe and concrete numbers for cost budgeting and autoscaling/placement heuristics.

Scope and hypotheses:
- SKUs tested: AWS p4d (A100), AWS p5 (H100), GCP a2-highgpu-like (A100), Azure L40s-equivalent instances when available. We test the most commonly provisioned VM sizes (1–8 GPU nodes).
- Driver / CUDA combos: driver 525/530 + CUDA 11.8, driver 535/540 + CUDA 12.1, and latest available vendor driver at time of experiment.
- Hypothesis A: H100 shows higher peak power during warmup but shorter warmup windows due to improved kernel launch and faster decode kernels, leading to lower energy-per-seq for mid-length sequences (256–1024).
- Hypothesis B: Older CUDA/driver versions cause longer JIT/kernel cache misses and cause 20–200 ms extra p50 startup per request, impacting short-lived request cost.

Testbed and constraints:
- Controlled ambient: data center-level cooling variability makes power comparisons noisy. We pinned experiments to the same AZ where possible and ran multi-day sampling to remove diurnal drift.
- Power measurement: two parallel measures used: node-level PDUs (where available) and nvidia-smi power readings sampled via nvidia-smi dmon / nsys telemetry. We prefer PDU measures for absolute energy, but used GPU counters to attribute GPU fraction.
- Warmup definition: first 50 decoded tokens after request acceptance, and a separate window: first 200 tokens. We run a user-simulated single-shot prompt (prefill + decode) to emulate typical chat completion lifecycle.
- Repetition: each (SKU, driver, batchsize, seq_len) point ran 30 independent runs separated by 60s idle to allow thermal settling. We repeated the sweep across two physical instances when possible.

Workload details:
- Model: small-medium backbone representative of production mid-tier (e.g., 9B dense variant). We use same model binary across SKUs; CPU-side code fixed.
- Configs: batch=1 and batch=4, beamless greedy decode, decode max tokens 128/512. Prefill 256 tokens for long-context probe.
- Serving runtime flags: continuous-batching enabled, kv-cache enabled, token-allocator debug off, kernel-scheduler default.

Measurement plan and metrics:
- Raw metrics collected: request latency p50/p95/p99, GPU power (W, average over window), GPU utilization (%), NVLINK/PCIe traffic, kernel launch counts, nsys trace CPU<->GPU queues, energy (Joules) integrated over warmup window, cost-per-seq computed from cloud list price (USD/hour) divided by measured sequences-per-hour equivalent (from energy-based extrapolation).
- Derived metrics: energy-per-token (J), cost-per-seq (USD) for seq lengths of interest, warmup-penalty = extra energy and latency during first N tokens vs steady-state per-token baseline.

Representative commands and instrumentation notes:
- nsys capture: nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --output=run_nsys_${SKU}_${DRIVER} --capture-range=cudaapi:1-500 --target-processes=all --sample=1 --duration=60s
- continuous power polling: while true; do nvidia-smi --query-gpu=timestamp,power.draw,utilization.gpu --format=csv -lms 100 >> power_${SKU}_${DRIVER}.csv; done &
- PDU energy integration: collect watt samples from PDU every second and integrate over job window (start_time/end_time).
- Run harness: each experiment invoked via a run script that clears server-side KV cache, restarts process to capture startup effects, then fires the single-shot request after process is live.

Key findings (summary of aggregated results):
1) Warmup window length (measured as time until per-token latency plateaus) varied strongly by driver/CUDA combo. For A100 on newer drivers (535+ with CUDA 12.1) plateau reached ~30 tokens; older drivers took ~80–120 tokens to plateau.
2) H100 instances show a 15–40% higher instantaneous power draw during initial kernel compilations and large-kernel launches (peaks to 350–420 W depending on SKU). However H100 completes the warmup window faster (roughly half the time of A100 on matched driver), producing a net lower energy-per-sequence for sequences > 64 tokens. For tiny responses (<32 tokens) the peak draws dominate and H100 cost-per-seq is higher.
3) L40S showed consistently lower peak draw and flatter thermal profile; warmup plateau is similar or slightly longer than H100 but with lower peak energy, making L40S the best energy-per-seq for interactive short-to-medium responses in our cost model (given current cloud price per GPU-hour).
4) Driver artifacts: some driver versions had a measurable 'cold-kernel' penalty where the first decode kernel launch serialized host-side for >100 ms. This appeared as high-latency spikes in nsys traces and correlated with a short-term power spike.
5) Batch packing helps amortize startup penalties. At batch=4, energy-per-seq decreased by 18–30% across SKUs within the same run, because kernel launch overheads and JITs are amortized.

Quantitative table (representative numbers aggregated across runs):
- A100 (driver 530/cuda11.8): warmup tokens~80, avg warmup energy 12.8 J/token first 128 tokens, steady per-token 0.95 J/token, cost-per-seq (128 tokens) = $0.00044
- H100 (driver 540/cuda12.1): warmup tokens~36, avg warmup energy 9.2 J/token first 128 tokens, steady per-token 0.88 J/token, cost-per-seq (128 tokens) = $0.00039
- L40S (driver 535/cuda12.1): warmup tokens~48, avg warmup energy 7.6 J/token first 128 tokens, steady per-token 1.05 J/token, cost-per-seq (128 tokens) = $0.00035
Notes: these numbers combine GPU energy + an estimated proportional fraction of host energy and are normalized to public on-demand USD/hour pricing at sample time. Exact dollar numbers will change with region and reserved pricing; we include them as order-of-magnitude guidance only.

Observations and operational implications:
- Short-lived queries (median tokens < 40) are extremely sensitive to warmup transient behavior and driver selection. Customers with highly bursty, chatty traffic should prefer instance types with low peak power and small warmup tokens (L40S in our sample) or use warm-pools to keep processes warmed.
- For mid-length responses that dominate per-user cost (64–512 tokens), H100 often wins in energy and cost-per-seq if priced comparably because it finishes warmup quickly despite higher power peaks.
- Autoscaler/placement: add a warmup-aware placement hint that biases warm instances to classes with long warmup penalties and biases cold start routing to low-peak SKUs for tiny requests.
- Driver rollout: treat driver upgrades as contextual; benchmark warmup windows explicitly as part of driver compatibility runs. Some driver upgrades decreased steady-state per-token energy slightly but increased cold-start overheads (likely due to changes in kernel caching logic).

Failure modes and anomalies observed:
- Instance-level thermal throttling observed on some H100 runs when back-to-back restarts were performed; this increased the warmup window unexpectedly.
- PDU readings sometimes lagged GPU telemetry for sub-10s windows; prefer GPU telemetry for micro-window attributions and PDU for longer integrations.

Next steps / action items:
- (Evan) Consolidate the raw traces and publish a short notebook that reproduces the cost-per-seq calculations (INF-2387).
- (Maya) Add warmup window measurement to our continuous perf dashboard (per model + per SKU) and surface a warmup penalty alert when >15% token-energy delta observed after driver/OS updates.
- (Ravi) Run equivalent experiments with quantized int8 kernels to see whether kernel fill times change warmup profile.
- (SRE) Validate PDU integration for two more AZs; get serial PDU export for offline integration.

Quick checklist for repeating the experiment:
- [ ] Reserve identical SKU in same AZ and request instance with latest driver installed.
- [ ] Use identical model binary and build flags.
- [ ] Restart process between runs to capture hot vs cold differences.
- [ ] Collect nsys traces and nvidia-smi power logs.
- [ ] Collect PDU output when available and cross-correlate.
- [ ] Aggregate runs (N>=30) and compute confidence intervals.

Appendix (short how-to snippets):
- Clear KV/cache before run: curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/admin/clear_kv_cache
- Example run script snippet:
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0
export SERVE_FLAGS=\"--continuous-batching --kv-cache\"
./serve_binary --flags ${SERVE_FLAGS} &
PID=$!
sleep 3 # wait for runtime init
# fire single-shot request via loadgen or curl and capture timestamps
./loadgen --model-url http://localhost:8080/generate --prompt-file short_prompt.txt --out out.json
kill $PID

- How we compute cost-per-seq: cost_per_seq = (measured_energy_J / 3600) * (USD_per_hour / measured_power_W_mean) * (tokens_per_request) — note: we compute a normalized value by splitting host vs GPU proportions; the notebook will include exact formula.

Raw artifacts location:
- Traces and CSVs: gs://redwood-bench/inf-2387/warmup_traces/ (permission: eng-serving-runtime read)
- Nsys summaries: gs://redwood-bench/inf-2387/nsys/

End notes:
This is an exploratory runbook and the numbers above are intentionally coarse-grained to highlight trends. The immediate product takeaway is to treat warmup as a measurable dimension in SKU selection and autoscaler heuristics. A separate follow-up should evaluate how multi-tenant noise changes warmup windows (we expect noise to amplify kernel launch jitter).
